comment: The Open Sicilian, as announced on the audio: 'on va apprendre à la jouer de manière ouverte' (let's learn to play it the open way).
The knight hits e4 at once, which is why White has to spend the next move on Nc3 rather than choosing a setup freely.
The Najdorf. ...a6 takes b5 away from White's knight and bishop and keeps ...e5 or ...b5 in reserve.

Solid but slow. In the 6.Bg5 h6 7.Bh4 e6 structure the usual plan is 8.f4 with Qf3 and long castling (+0.4 at depth 18 against +0.2 for Be2): the pawn supports e5 and f5 and keeps the h4 bishop's pin relevant.
Black breaks the pin on f6 and gets ready to castle short. The h4 bishop now has no pin to exploit and stands undefended (the e2 bishop blocks the queen).
Black keeps the extra pawn and the bishop pair (-1.9). White's compensation has to come from development and the open d-file.
The right order: trade on c6 first. With the knight still on d4, Nxd6+ Bxd6 Qxd6 Qxd6 Rxd6 would end with the c6 knight taking on d4.
Material is level again, but the structure has turned: an isolated c6 pawn, a weak a6 pawn and a king still in the centre (+2.4).
He reads the new structure correctly: 'Du coup maintenant il a un pion isolé' (now he has an isolated pawn). The c6 pawn is the target for the next ten moves.
Taking the queens makes White's d-file pressure easier to use. 15...Bb7 was a little more stubborn (+2.3 against +2.6).
As predicted on the audio ('il va faire dame prend'), the queens came off and the rook lands on d6 eyeing both c6 and a6.
White is a clean pawn up (6 against 5) with a 3-to-1 queenside majority, and Black's h8 rook and king are still undeveloped (+3.9).
Back to a8 to hold a6: the rook that went to d8 two moves ago has gone round in a circle.
The engine's first choice too. His reasoning: bring the second rook to attack a6, 'il a du retard de développement, j'abuse de ça' (he's behind in development, I'm exploiting it).
Castling finally activates the h8 rook, but 20...a5 first (+3.9 against +4.2) got the pawn off the square the rooks were aiming at.
Doubling on the a6 pawn: 'je devrais pouvoir manger le pion sans angoisse' (I should be able to take the pawn without worry). At depth 18 Rdd6 and Rd4 are equal (+3.6).
The pawn steps out of the double attack. On a5 it can no longer be hit by rooks along the sixth rank.

He saw it straight away: 'ça n'attaque pas le pion... il ne se passe rien' (it doesn't attack the pawn, nothing happens). Harmless though: +4.3 against +4.4 for 22.c4, and the rook offers the a-file trade on White's terms.

Good decision-making. He considered a4 and swinging a rook back to win a5, spotted that Black would then take the other rook, and chose b3: luft for the king, support for c4, and a path Kb2-a3 towards a5. The engine's first choice (+4.9, trading on a8 at once +4.6).
Black's only plan: bring the king to the centre and towards f2, since the rooks alone cannot hold the queenside.

He debated collecting a5 with the king against pushing c4 at once. The engine sees no difference (Kb2 and c4 both +5.1 in the sweep, +4.0 at depth 20), and its main line after Kb2 plays c4 two moves later anyway: the pawns matter more than the a5 pawn.
The king heads for e4 and f2. 24...Kf6 was a shade tighter (+5.2 against +5.4), but this is the race that decides the game.
Trading rooks is best (+5.4, 25.c4 +5.0). Of the follow-ups he named, the engine at depth 20 ranks 26.c4 +4.0, 26.Rd7 +3.7 and 26.Rd4 +2.9: Rd4 is the one to avoid.

'On y va maintenant sur c4 pour mettre la pression' (let's go c4 now to put on pressure): the engine's first choice (+4.0 at depth 20, 26.a3 clearly weaker). His worry that 26.Rd4 lets ...e5 gain time was correct, it drops to +2.9.
Black's counterplay: kingside pawns supported by the king. 26...Ke4 at once was about the same (+5.5 against +5.7).
'On va faire a3, b4 et on pousse nos deux pions' (a3, b4 and push both pawns): a3 prepares b4 to dissolve a5 and leave two connected passed pawns. Level with the engine's 27.Kc3 (+5.8 both).
Two connected passed pawns on b4 and c4 against Black's king and kingside pawns. From here it is a tempo count, and White's pawns are closer.
The king goes for f2, trading its defensive role for a passed pawn of its own.
'J'aurais pu faire c5 tout à l'heure' (I could have played c5 earlier): correct, 28.c5 was the engine's first choice (+6.0 against +5.7 for b4). Now it is also best (+6.7).
Tempo count: c7 is next, while Black's most advanced pawn still needs four moves to queen.
The rook blockades on c8, but it now has to watch c7 and the b-pawn at the same time.
Rook behind the passed pawn: Rc1 defends c7 from behind and frees the b-pawn to run.
The second pawn runs; one rook cannot stop two connected pawns on the seventh and fifth ranks.
b7 hits c8, so Black has to give the rook for the c-pawn.
Trading rooks first is the clean route. 38.b8=Q at once allows ...Rxc1 and leaves White fighting the e-pawn with a queen (+11.7 instead of a forced mate).
Check first, then the rook gets behind the e-pawn.
Re7 stops the e-pawn from behind and b8=Q follows. Black resigned.
